pos: n. (proper name; the spy from Zebulun)
etymology: Hebrew Gaddi'el, God is my fortune, from gad, fortune or troop, and 'el, God.
biblical_def: Gaddiel is the man of Zebulun sent among the twelve to search the land of Canaan: “Of the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel the son of Sodi” (Numbers 13:10). He is named once and never again, and the silence is the verdict. The twelve went up as rulers of their tribes, saw the same land, carried back the same cluster of grapes, and ten of them said, “We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we” (Numbers 13:31). Caleb and Joshua alone are remembered for faith; the other ten, Gaddiel among them, “died by the plague before the LORD” (Numbers 14:37). His name confesses that God is his portion, and his report denied it. Scripture keeps the list so that the reader will know that unbelief had names, tribes, and fathers, and that office in the congregation is no proof of faith in the God of the promise.

corruption_summary: The ten spies are often excused as realists giving an honest military estimate; Scripture calls their report an evil report and unbelief.
corruption_paragraphs: A common modern reading treats the ten as prudent men whose caution was simply outvoted by two optimists. The text does not allow it. Their estimate of the Anakim was accurate; their conclusion was not, because it left the LORD out of the reckoning. Moses calls it a slander upon the land, and God answers it with death in the wilderness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that unbelief is not a temperament but a sin. Hebrews draws the line plainly: they could not enter in because of unbelief. A leader who counts the giants and forgets the promise does not lead the people anywhere but back toward Egypt.

pos: n. (proper name; the spy from Manasseh)
biblical_def: Gaddi is the ruler of Manasseh among the twelve spies: “Of the tribe of Joseph, namely, of the tribe of Manasseh, Gaddi the son of Susi” (Numbers 13:11). The tribe of Joseph sent two men, one from Ephraim and one from Manasseh, for the double portion that Jacob gave to Joseph's sons was already shaping the order of the camp. Ephraim's man was Oshea the son of Nun, whom Moses renamed Jehoshua, Joshua; Manasseh's man was Gaddi. Two brothers' houses, two spies, and two opposite ends: Joshua led Israel across the Jordan, and Gaddi “died by the plague before the LORD” (Numbers 14:37). The same blessing on the same father did not make the same men. Every one of the twelve had a lineage worth boasting of, and only two had faith.

corruption_paragraphs: Gaddi and Joshua came from the two halves of Joseph's house, the most honoured line in Israel after Judah. The text refuses to let that honour decide anything. One spy believed God and inherited; the other doubted and fell.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that covenant privilege heightens responsibility rather than replacing it. To be born in the house of blessing and to die in unbelief is the warning that runs from the wilderness to the Epistle to the Hebrews.

pos: n. (proper name; father of the spy from Dan)
etymology: Hebrew Gemalli, perhaps camel-owner or my recompense, from gamal, to deal fully with, to recompense, or gamal, camel.
biblical_def: Gemalli is named only as a father: “Of the tribe of Dan, Ammiel the son of Gemalli” (Numbers 13:12). His son was Dan's ruler among the twelve sent to search Canaan, and the son's name, Ammiel, means people of God — a name his report did not honour, for Ammiel was among the ten whose word turned the camp back toward Egypt. Gemalli himself is otherwise unknown. His single mention belongs to a pattern in Numbers, where the fathers are recorded with the sons so that each tribe's responsibility is fixed to a house. Israel did not fall in the wilderness as an anonymous mass. Each tribe sent a named ruler, the son of a named father, and each tribe's ruler answered for his report.

pos: n. (proper name; the spy from Gad)
etymology: Hebrew Ge'u'el, majesty of God, from ge'ut, majesty, pride, and 'el, God.
biblical_def: Geuel is the ruler of Gad sent among the twelve spies: “Of the tribe of Gad, Geuel the son of Machi” (Numbers 13:15). He is the last-named of the ten who returned with the evil report, and the irony of his name is sharp: a man called the majesty of God came back from Canaan magnifying the Anakim instead. The ten said, “all the people that we saw in it are men of a great stature” (Numbers 13:32), and in their own eyes they were as grasshoppers. Gad's later history makes the contrast plainer, for the tribe whose spy feared the land would ask to settle on the east side of Jordan, and Moses would require its men of war to cross over armed before their brethren until the land was subdued. Geuel saw the giants and forgot whose majesty his name confessed.

pos: n. (proper name; prince of Benjamin for the dividing of Canaan)
etymology: Hebrew 'Elidad, God has loved, from 'el, God, and dod, beloved.
biblical_def: Elidad is the prince of Benjamin appointed, before Israel crossed the Jordan, to divide the land by lot: “Of the tribe of Benjamin, Elidad the son of Chislon” (Numbers 34:21). The list in Numbers 34 is the hopeful counterpart of the list in Numbers 13. Forty years earlier twelve rulers searched the land and ten refused it; now, with that generation buried, the LORD names a new set of princes to apportion an inheritance not yet conquered, because He regards it as already given. “These are they whom the LORD commanded to divide the inheritance unto the children of Israel in the land of Canaan” (Numbers 34:29). Elidad's appointment is an act of faith on God's part before it is an act of administration on Israel's: the surveyor is commissioned while the Canaanite still holds the field. His name, God has loved, fits the occasion, for the inheritance rested on electing love and not on Benjamin's strength.

corruption_summary: The conquest is read as a land-grab dressed in religion; Numbers presents the inheritance as the LORD's gift, divided by His command before it was taken.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern readings often treat the allotment of Canaan as a later ideology projected back onto tribal migrations. Numbers 34 reads the other way: the boundaries, the princes and the method of division are all given by God before a single city falls, so that Israel receives the land as a gift rather than seizing it as a prize.

The principle to recover is that inheritance in Scripture is grace before it is possession. The princes did not decide who deserved what; they cast the lot before the LORD, and the disposing thereof was His. The same pattern governs the believer's inheritance, reserved in heaven and given, not earned.

pos: n. (proper name; prince of Manasseh for the dividing of Canaan)
etymology: Hebrew Channi'el, grace of God, from chen, grace, favour, and 'el, God.
biblical_def: Hanniel is the prince of Manasseh named for the division of the land: “The prince of the children of Joseph, for the tribe of the children of Manasseh, Hanniel the son of Ephod” (Numbers 34:23). He stands in the place Gaddi held forty years before. Gaddi was Manasseh's spy, who searched the land and refused it; Hanniel is Manasseh's prince, who receives it by lot. Between the two lists lies a generation's grave in the wilderness, and the difference in their names is a small sermon: one called my fortune trusted his own estimate, the other called the grace of God divides an inheritance that grace alone could give. Hanniel is otherwise unknown. A different Haniel, spelled with one n in the King James text, is an Asherite in 1 Chronicles 7:39.

pos: n. (proper name; a king of Midian slain in the war of vengeance)
etymology: Hebrew 'Evi, perhaps desire; the meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Evi is the first-named of the five kings of Midian slain when Israel avenged the matter of Peor: “they slew the kings of Midian, beside the rest of them that were slain; namely, Evi, and Rekem, and Zur, and Hur, and Reba, five kings of Midian: Balaam also the son of Beor they slew with the sword” (Numbers 31:8). Joshua 13:21 calls the same five princes of Midian and dukes of Sihon. The war was not a raid for spoil. Midian had followed Balaam's counsel and drawn Israel into whoredom and the worship of Baal-peor, and Moses says plainly, “these caused the children of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to commit trespass against the LORD in the matter of Peor” (Numbers 31:16). Evi died beside the prophet who had taught his people how to destroy Israel when cursing could not. Balaam's end with the kings of Midian shows where his counsel had always belonged.

corruption_summary: The Midianite war is cited as divine genocide; the text presents it as judgment on a nation that made itself Israel's seducer.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 31 is a favourite text for critics who charge the God of Israel with cruelty. The chapter itself names the cause: Midian beguiled Israel with wiles, by Balaam's counsel, to commit trespass in the matter of Peor, and twenty-four thousand died of the plague for it. The war was the LORD's vengeance on the seducer, not an act of conquest.

The principle to recover is that God judges nations as well as persons, and that He reckons the corruption of His people as warfare against Himself. Balaam's death among the kings of Midian is the commentary on his career: the prophet who could not curse Israel taught its enemies how to make Israel curse itself.

pos: n. (proper name; king of Hebron in the days of Joshua)
biblical_def: Hoham is the king of Hebron summoned into the southern coalition against Gibeon: “Wherefore Adonizedek king of Jerusalem sent unto Hoham king of Hebron, and unto Piram king of Jarmuth, and unto Japhia king of Lachish, and unto Debir king of Eglon, saying” (Joshua 10:3). Gibeon had made peace with Israel by craft, and the five kings resolved to punish it. Joshua came up from Gilgal all night, the LORD cast great hailstones from heaven, and the sun stood still upon Gibeon. The five kings hid in a cave at Makkedah; Joshua brought them out, had his captains set their feet upon their necks, and “afterward Joshua smote them, and slew them, and hanged them on five trees” (Joshua 10:26). Hebron, Hoham's city, was afterward given to Caleb, the spy who had believed when the city was a stronghold of the Anakim.

pos: n. (proper name; king of Gezer slain by Joshua)
biblical_def: Horam is the king of Gezer who marched to relieve Lachish when Joshua besieged it: “Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish; and Joshua smote him and his people, until he had left him none remaining” (Joshua 10:33). He was not one of the five kings of the cave but a neighbour who came late to a lost cause, and the list of conquered kings records him plainly: “The king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one” (Joshua 12:12). Yet Gezer itself was not taken, for Ephraim “drave not out the Canaanites that dwelt in Gezer”, and the city remained Canaanite until a Pharaoh burned it and gave it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife. Horam's defeat shows that a king can be slain while his city is spared through Israel's slackness; the victory God gave was not followed through, and the leftover Canaanite became a thorn.

pos: n. (proper name; king of the Zidonians, father of Jezebel)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ethba'al, with Baal, from 'eth, with, and ba'al, lord, the name of the Phoenician storm-god.
biblical_def: Ethbaal is the king of the Zidonians whose daughter Ahab married: “he took to wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, and went and served Baal, and worshipped him” (1 Kings 16:31). The verse ties the marriage and the idolatry into a single act, and Scripture treats it as worse than Jeroboam's calves — “as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam”, Ahab went further. Ethbaal's name means with Baal, and his daughter carried his religion into Samaria with her: a temple and altar of Baal, four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and four hundred of the groves eating at her table, and the prophets of the LORD hunted to death. The king of Tyre and Zidon never set foot in Israel; his daughter did his work there. Revelation 2:20 takes her name as a byword for a seducing prophetess in the church.

corruption_summary: Ahab's marriage is read as shrewd foreign policy; Scripture reads it as the door through which Baal entered Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: Historians rightly note that the alliance with Tyre brought Israel trade and prestige. The book of Kings does not dispute the fact; it simply refuses to count it as gain. The marriage is reported in the same breath as the worship of Baal, because the one carried the other.

The principle to recover is that marriage outside the faith is never merely a private or political matter. The law forbade it because it turns away the heart, and Ethbaal's daughter is the case in point: none was like Ahab, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up.

roots_lines: Hebrew 'Ethba'al, from 'eth, with, and ba'al, lord.
King of the Zidonians in the days of Ahab.
Father of Jezebel, Ahab's wife (1 Kings 16:31).
His daughter brought Baal's prophets and altar into Samaria.
Jezebel's name became a byword in Revelation 2:20.
